item.title: Google alternative Kagi launches an email service
item.description: Kagi, which already offers a paid alternative to Google Search and its own Orion browser as a rival to Chrome, is taking on another Google service: Gmail. Today, Kagi announced a public beta of Kagi Mail, a new email service that has "no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in." With Kagi Mail, you get an @ kagimail.com address, but the service also supports unlimited aliases and domains. It also offers 50GB of storage and a built-in calendar. On the roadmap, you can expect contacts and an address book in Q1 2027, but native mobile apps aren't expected to arrive until Q3 2027. "Does the world need another email service? item.title: The hacker behind early GTA VI leaks has been sentenced — and released
item.description: Arion Kurtaj, who pleaded guilty last week to hacking Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games and other companies, including Uber and Revolut, was sentenced to seven years in prison but released on license , the BBC reports . After hacking Rockstar, Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI in 2022, years before the game's public release last week. Prior to his sentencing, Kurtaj had already spent time in a hospital because of his autism and in prison. "You are obviously a very talented young man," the judge in the case said, according to Sky News . "Don't waste those talents by spending the rest of your life in and out of prison." item.title: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
item.description: A Windows version of Ladybird is coming in the “later stages” of the project. | Image: Ladybird Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling announced that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development. The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We've seen many engines emerge over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. While Gecko, now used in Mozilla Firefox, first appeared in Netscape 6 in 2000 , Apple's WebKit arrived in Safari in 2003 as a fork of KDE's KHTML. item.title: Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
item.description: After Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO , following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith's radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would "end up on his feet." "You know the expression, anybody can be replaced," Trump said, floating Apple's ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate. It didn't take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he'd welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia's own board wasn't ready to do so. Behind the scen … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes
item.description: Share price surges as chipmaker reverses decision to remove chief executive after US president ‘convinced’ its board Comment: Nvidia’s humiliated board should resign out of embarrassment US politics – live updates Timeline: fall and comeback of Jensen Huang Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after Donald Trump directly intervened with the US AI chipmaker’s board of directors, in a stunning reversal of the tech billionaire’s downfall . Speaking on Monday shortly after Nvidia’s surprise announcement that Huang had been restored to the top job – less than two weeks after he resigned – Trump said that he had “convinced” the board to do it. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC. Huang had resigned after reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees. Continue reading...

item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next?
item.description: After the leather-jacketed CEO, president, and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, his company initially announced an investigation. However, after The New York Times reported there was evidence of another affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him, a board meeting that night ended with Huang’s resignation , and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was installed as the new interim CEO. And then… Huang was back. In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies. Saying it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia’s board announced his return as CEO on November 23rd, less than two weeks after his resignation. Follow along below for all of the latest updates. Jensen Huang says he’ll be a ‘better CEO’ as staff applauds his return How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again Jensen Huang has already come back to Nvidia’s offices. White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia’s CEO Trump says reinstating Jensen Huang “would be the best thing” for Nvidia and the US. Arm CEO Rene Haas isn’t jumping ship to lead Nvidia. More details emerge regarding the extent of Alice Huang’s alleged spying. Nvidia’s stock closes the week down 14 percent, as Reuters reports the SEC is looking into its “accounting practices.” Jensen Huang reportedly “terrorized” Nvidia employees. item.title: Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang
item.description: Too big to fail, the sequel. | Image: The Verge; Getty Images I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened. item.title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
item.description: President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January. The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP). Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation. Read full article Comments

item.title: Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week
item.description: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI , resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register ’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI , resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register ’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting , digital extortion, real-life shootings , and other physical violence . Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com , along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.” Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®

item.title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
item.description: The Apple Watch Series 12 is on sale in multiple configurations. | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $299 ($100 off) at Amazon and Walmart , beating its most sale price by $30. If you prefer a larger size, the 46mm model is on sale for $349 ($100 off) at Amazon and Walmart , beating its previous low by $30. Apple Watch Series 12 Where to Buy: $399 $299 at Amazon (GPS, 42mm) $399 $299 at Walmart (GPS, 42mm) $449 $349 at Amazon (GPS, 46mm) The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around. It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day. Read our Apple Watch Series 12 review . Apple Watch Series 12 Where to Buy: $399 $299 at Amazon (GPS, 42mm) $399 $299 at Walmart (GPS, 42mm) $449 $349 at Amazon (GPS, 46mm) The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around. It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day. item.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
item.description: On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children. SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM). Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked . Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first , Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today. Read full article Comments

item.title: Amazon scoops up AI accelerator tech to keep chips busy at all times
item.description: Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations. The house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold. Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.” DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.” Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs. An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full company acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back. Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications. Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion. If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM . ®

item.title: Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it's a big secret
item.description: It was the most simple of questions. On Monday afternoon, during a NASA news conference about the International Space Station, Space News reporter Jeff Foust asked about an upcoming launch of a Russian spacecraft. "It's my understanding there's another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress," Foust said. "Can you confirm that, and give the date and time that will launch?" This Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday. It is going to a space station co-operated by the US space agency. But no, NASA would not provide this basic information about the upcoming Progress launch. Read full article Comments

item.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
item.description: “It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want. But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age. Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history , smart devices , and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price. Read full article Comments

item.title: Amazon fights Delivery Protection Act by putting stickers on its packages
item.description: Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill. This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for New Yorkers.” Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518 ), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries. Read full article Comments

item.title: Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them
item.description: Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions. Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate. The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him. “It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote . That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair. For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote. Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it. Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige. “What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing. Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them. Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions. Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate. The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him. “It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote . That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair. For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote. Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it. Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige. “What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing. Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them. Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked. “The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair said. “It said yes to four bytes from a total stranger then energised several tonnes’ worth of brakes and reported back that it had done so, pleased with itself.” Further experiments managed to modify braking strength based on deceleration speed as well, making it so that the trailer acted unpredictably based on the amount of force a driver applied to stop their vehicle. To say this is worse than a typical internet-connected device bug is to put it mildly - it even earned a trio of CVEs from CISA, with two of them scoring a CVSS of 9.6. “The attack surface is ‘anyone within Bluetooth range,’ the skill required is ‘can write four bytes,’ and the victim selection is ‘optional,’ ” Forck and McCarthy said. The fact AI was able to get them to that point in just a couple of days is even more concerning, they added. “This kind of research used to require a fairly rare and specific skill set,” the pair noted. “It now requires curiosity, a device you own, and an AI that can read bytecode faster than any human.” Luckily, they appear to have been dealing with a relatively responsive company in Elecbrakes - patches have been deployed for both the in-car and trailer-mounted models of their brake controllers. Installation is a manual process, we note, so if you own a controller from the company, be sure to stop and install the update. Unfortunately, Elecbrakes has a third controller out there that hasn’t been manufactured in several years, and it got skipped in the patching process. Owners of an ELBC2000 should be aware that their controller is still vulnerable, and there’s no patch available yet, as the vendor didn’t confirm that the ELBC2000 was vulnerable until the end of October, after it faced pressure from the researchers. ®

item.title: Reports: Russia may launch nuclear weapon into orbit as soon as next month
item.description: Western intelligence officials worry that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit before the end of the year, suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought, German media reported Monday. The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites. US lawmakers briefed on government intelligence first disclosed Russia's ambition to deploy a space-based nuclear weapon in early 2024 . At the time, US officials said Russia had launched a test satellite in 2022 to test the effects of radiation on space hardware and pave the way for a future nuclear-armed craft, but that Russia had not yet sent a nuclear weapon into orbit. Read full article Comments

item.title: Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
item.description: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers. CVE-2026-76466 , which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services. The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments. “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.” At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability. That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information. The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6. The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices. A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday. Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®
item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers. CVE-2026-76466 , which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services. The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments. “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.” At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability. That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information. The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6. The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices. A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday. Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®

item.title: Bulgaria evicts cyber snoops who lurked inside government networks for 5 years
item.description: The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration. Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021. It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a new, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer. "The incident was discovered thanks to the new national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added. "Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time." Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise. Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages. The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers. The ministry said that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access. Vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved. In a follow-up interview with bTV , Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected. A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen." Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®

item.title: How freaked out should we be? After mass outages, experts tell us how close we are to ‘doomsday’
item.description: As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly. Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure. Continue reading...

item.title: Microsoft mega outage: Report reveals testing gaps and emails that never arrived
item.description: Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures. The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected users, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer. A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's plans to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments. The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14. Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The company said all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost. The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US users came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive. The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix. Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising. Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom. Microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now plans to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing. Microsoft also plans to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®

item.title: Marvel crams every superhero ever into Avengers: Doomsday final trailer
item.description: Rumors have been swirling for days that we would be getting a final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday , the penultimate film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s Phase Six, heralding the end of the so-called “Multiverse Saga.” The rumors were true: Marvel just released the trailer, featuring pretty much every superhero ever represented in the MCU. And it looks like the Avengers will face consequences for messing with the timeline to reverse the blip in Endgame . As previously reported , the film takes place 14 months after the events of Thunderbolts* . Per the official logline: “Beloved heroes from three distinct universes will be set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they’ve ever encountered.” Those universes are Earth-616 (the Avengers, Wakandans, and New Avengers), Earth-828 (Fantastic Four), and the “original” X-Men. Cast-wise, we have Avengers favorites Thor (Chris Hemsworth), the new Captain America (Anthony Mackie), Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Falcon (Danny Ramirez), and Loki (Tom Hiddleston). Then there’s the Wakandan contingent: Shuri as the new Black Panther (Letitia Wright), M’Baku (Winston Duke), and Namor (Tenoch Huerta Mejia), as well as Alex Livinalli as Namor’s ally, Attuma. And, of course, Robert Downey Jr. as Doctor Doom. Read full article Comments

item.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair
item.description: Nvidia's board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is "effective immediately" and was based in part on "input from senior levels of the United States government" that assured the board members that "Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk." That assurance comes despite Huang's admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Read full article Comments

item.title: COP31 ends in failure as countries split over fossil fuels, climate finance
item.description: ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams. As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization, and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism. Many countries were not buying it. Read full article Comments

item.title: British retailer Next downplays data breach at tech supplier
item.description: British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about. The clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next. The retailer says its own systems remain untouched and that, so far, there's no evidence that customer personal data has fallen into the wrong hands. "We have been informed that one of our third-party online suppliers has experienced a cyber incident which has resulted in unauthorized access to certain benign data relating to NEXT," the company said in its statement, which it shared with The Register . "We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier." The breached supplier provides technology services to Next, and the "benign" information accessed is understood to be low-level data. Sensitive customer details, including addresses, passwords, and banking information, are believed to be unaffected. Next hasn't identified the supplier, explained exactly what the hackers managed to get their hands on, or revealed how much information was accessed, and declined to say when asked by The Register . However, the retailer has seemingly decided that the stolen data won’t be of much use to the criminals responsible. "Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised," Next said. "The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or NEXT." Next also stressed that its own IT infrastructure had escaped unscathed, saying it was "confident that NEXT’s own systems have not been compromised and that this remains an incident affecting the supplier's environment." Despite repeatedly describing the compromised information as harmless, Next says it is treating the incident "with the utmost seriousness" and is working with the affected supplier, law enforcement, and relevant regulators. The incident comes just weeks after fellow British fashion retailer Asos suffered a breach of its own , with hackers gaining access to customer information through third-party platforms. That attack, which came to light on October 6 when customers received an unauthorized push notification through the Asos app announcing that the company had been hacked, was traced to a social engineering scam. An attacker impersonated a trusted contact to trick an Asos employee into handing over login credentials, which were then used to access external platforms. Asos later admitted that the intruders had accessed customer names, contact details, and some account information, but passwords and payment card details were apparently off limits. Next reckons its customers have been luckier, but there’s a lot

item.title: Nvidia board puts Jensen Huang back as boss
item.description: There's no telling what caused the Nvidia board to vote unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO less than a week after saying his return wasn’t under consideration – except reportedly the threat of having one's head ripped off and brain peed on – but that really doesn't matter, at least as far as shareholders need to be concerned: Jensen's back in charge and all’s right in the world of chip stocks. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said of the decision to reinstate him, calling it an honor. Nvidia kicked its former-cum-current CEO and president to the curb on November 12, but not over allegations that he may have been sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy – it was affairs at Nvidia with his subordinates that appears to have been the last straw with Nvidia directors. Nvidia stock has tumbled since Huang’s ouster, and much of the rest of the tech stock world followed suit . Nvidia insiders and tech heavyweights have been pushing for Huang’s return for about as long as he was unemployed, but calls for his return from the US federal government may have been the catalyst for a change of heart among Nvidia leadership who didn’t want Huang back. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," Nvidia said in its statement announcing Huang’s return. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones added. Jones was made Nvidia's first board chair upon Huang’s resignation, and will remain in that role. The White House has since confirmed that the senior-level official involved in Huang’s reinstatement was President Trump. According to a White House statement to Semafor, Trump personally dialed in to an Nvidia board meeting hours before Huang was reinstated to argue for his return. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House comms director Steven Cheung told Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.” "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. "The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." The surprise return echoes Sam Altman's return as CEO of OpenAI after the board fired him for a brief five days in 2023 over allegations of dishonesty. Both reinstatements happened around the US Thanksgiving holiday, suggesting that the spirit of forgiveness waxes with the anticipation of that roasted turkey smell wafting through the house. ® Updated at 1607 GMT to include the fact that Trump dialed into a board m
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: There's no telling what caused the Nvidia board to vote unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO less than a week after saying his return wasn’t under consideration – except reportedly the threat of having one's head ripped off and brain peed on – but that really doesn't matter, at least as far as shareholders need to be concerned: Jensen's back in charge and all’s right in the world of chip stocks. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said of the decision to reinstate him, calling it an honor. Nvidia kicked its former-cum-current CEO and president to the curb on November 12, but not over allegations that he may have been sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy – it was affairs at Nvidia with his subordinates that appears to have been the last straw with Nvidia directors. Nvidia stock has tumbled since Huang’s ouster, and much of the rest of the tech stock world followed suit . Nvidia insiders and tech heavyweights have been pushing for Huang’s return for about as long as he was unemployed, but calls for his return from the US federal government may have been the catalyst for a change of heart among Nvidia leadership who didn’t want Huang back. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," Nvidia said in its statement announcing Huang’s return. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones added. Jones was made Nvidia's first board chair upon Huang’s resignation, and will remain in that role. The White House has since confirmed that the senior-level official involved in Huang’s reinstatement was President Trump. According to a White House statement to Semafor, Trump personally dialed in to an Nvidia board meeting hours before Huang was reinstated to argue for his return. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House comms director Steven Cheung told Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.” "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. "The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." The surprise return echoes Sam Altman's return as CEO of OpenAI after the board fired him for a brief five days in 2023 over allegations of dishonesty. Both reinstatements happened around the US Thanksgiving holiday, suggesting that the spirit of forgiveness waxes with the anticipation of that roasted turkey smell wafting through the house. ® Updated at 1607 GMT to include the fact that Trump dialed into a board meeting.

item.title: Everything going down at once wasn't evidence of a conspiracy – but the truth may be scarier
item.description: Have you or someone you love been affected by a tech outage this week? Yeah, us too. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live In a week of big stories the biggest one seems to be the fact that everyone from Microsoft to the NSA was dealing with outages , and here's what might be the worst part: It doesn't seem to be AI, nor hostile countries intent on destroying our infrastructure. Unfortunately for all of us, what the past week of outages reveal is that – as we discussed on The Kettle less than a month ago – all of our essential tech infrastructure is basically held together with duct tape and twine. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo , cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons , and open source reporter Liam Proven to discuss what comes next, and whether we can fix any of this without tearing all of it out and starting from scratch. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:04) Hi everyone and welcome to the latest episode of the Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and if you're hearing this, then that means there isn't an outage right now, which seems like that might be a lot to ask of our technology in the past week. It's been a busy week. We had Anthropic's IPO , Nvidia drama continuing , and other stuff going on. But the one thing that everyone seems to be talking about is what's become known in the zeitgeist as Outagepalooza, as it seems like everything was offline at some point in the past few days. With me to discuss the chaos and the conspiracy theories they're giving rise to is Reg cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons and our open source reporter Liam Proven. Guys, what's happening? Jessica Lyons (00:45) I've got my tinfoil hat on right now, so I'm ready. Brandon (00:48) Yes, I've had family calling me being like, my god, what's happening? Who's ending the world right now? Is it AI? Jessica Lyons (00:55) Ha ha ha. Brandon (00:56) We'll get to that part. Liam Proven (00:57) Wonderful. My mum's wardrobe door stuck this week and we found a company on the little rock in the middle of the Irish Sea that fixes sliding doors and he didn't get my emails because he's one hundred percent Microsoft and he uses Hotmail and it's Hotmail. Liam Proven (01:18) And when I got it through, you'd be amazed at the ramifications. I SMS'd him in the end and he got that and then was really angry because I said, "Dude, I've been trying to get you for three days. Can you at least reply and say Friday?" And he's like, "No, I've got no email, I've got no internet, I've got nothing." Brandon (01:32) My god. Yes, it's been an interesting week. So Jess, catch us up on everything that's fallen apart in the past few days. We've got quite a list growing here. Jessica Lyons (01:40) Yes. Well, we'll start with Outlook. I'm sorry, Mic

It's not intentional. It just becomes one by volume. Liam Proven (07:22) So it's actually becoming a little bit moot what exactly constitutes a denial of service attack versus merely being under extremely heavy load. I'm

item.title: F1 in Las Vegas: You've never seen an F1 race like this before
item.description: Las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023 , the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing. The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very quickly , leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor. But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle . Read full article Comments

item.title: Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad
item.description: US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China. Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose. Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country." The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said. The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X. We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer. Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here." The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week. "We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added. Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it. Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses. Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat. "There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register . "So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences." Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the c

"So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences." Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the cloud giants operate datacenters outside the US, such as latency and regulatory compliance. "A buyer in Frankfurt won't wait for a page to load from Virginia. Some countries require certain data to stay inside their borders, and big European clients write it into contracts anyway," he stated. Trump claimed that communities in America that host datacenters are "making so much money that they don't know what to do with it." Those claimed benefits come alongside substantial public subsidies. Nonprofit organization Good Jobs First reported earlier this year that some states are losing billions in revenue because of the tax abatement schemes offered to companies to entice them to set up shop there. ®

item.title: New Outlook's attachment issues sent users into the arms of its predecessor
item.description: A recent update broke attachment handling for some New Outlook users, prompting Microsoft to recommend switching to the web or Classic version of its email client. Things are going swimmingly for New Outlook, the email client that Microsoft would very much like users to migrate to. A code change meant that for some users, opening or uploading email attachments failed. It took the company two attempts to fix the problem. Microsoft confirmed there were issues on November 20, as reports that customers were having problems with attachments began rolling in. By the end of the day, the company had added inline images in email to the litany of woe and "paused the rollout of a recent client update that may be contributing to attachment failures." The advice for affected users was to switch to the web version, or use Outlook Classic to open or upload attachments and view inline images. The good news was that Microsoft produced a fix. The bad news was that this fix only resolved problems with Office attachments and inline images, leaving other attachment types affected, according to incident notice EX1561765. The Windows behemoth tried again with a "supplemental fix" and reported the remaining problems resolved on November 21. Users needed to close and reopen New Outlook for the fix to take effect. Microsoft said it had tested the fixes before deployment. Administrators might reasonably wish the original update had received the same attention. The preliminary root cause was a "recent update to the code which supports embedded web content unexpectedly caused impact." The clock is ticking for Outlook Classic. Microsoft is clear that New Outlook is the future, though Classic Outlook will remain available until at least 2029. The fact that the company had to suggest that affected users fall back on the old warhorse to perform that rarely used email activity – attachment handling – is less than confidence-inspiring. Still, by the time Outlook Classic is finally put out to pasture, we're sure Microsoft's habit of sending out broken updates will also be a thing of the past. Right? ®

item.title: Norway links energy firm cyberattacks to critical Azure API Management flaw
item.description: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations. According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register , Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies , only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2. It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault. Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration. The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs. Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote . "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets. The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise. NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations. The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation. "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said . "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. "When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses." Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear. Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day. The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise. NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations. The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation. "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said . "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. "When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses." Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear. Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day. The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied. NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched. Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

item.title: Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI
item.description: Buying a new computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense . Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia's new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models. While it doesn't have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16 , with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you're looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error. The PC stuff Before we dive into the AI agents, let's talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia's pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn't skimp on the specs. Read full article Comments

item.title: Cleverbridge admits attackers stole customers' credit card and CVV numbers. Yep, you read that right
item.description: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization. The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update , Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems. The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register , fills in some rather important blanks. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers. Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach. More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach. Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk. That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems. In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion. Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase. Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®
